t.3.64.1: Bṛhadaśva said: When that serpent had vanished, Nala of Niṣadha set out, and on the tenth day he entered the city of Ṛtuparṇa.
t.3.64.2: He approached the king, saying, "I am Bāhuka; skilled in the driving of horses, there is no one on earth equal to me."
t.3.64.3: I am also the one to be consulted in difficult affairs and in matters requiring skill, and I know the art of preparing food better than others.
t.3.64.4: Whatever crafts there are in this world, and whatever else is very difficult to do, all of that I shall strive to accomplish; Ṛtuparṇa, take me into your service.
t.3.64.5: Stay, Bāhuka, good fortune to you; you shall do all this. My mind is always set especially on swift driving.
t.3.64.6: So apply that skill of yours by which my horses would become swift. You are the overseer of my horses, and your wage is a hundred hundreds.
t.3.64.7: And these two, Vārṣṇeya and Jīvala, will always attend upon you; you will take your pleasure together with them. Dwell with me, Bāhuka.
t.3.64.8: Bṛhadaśva said: Thus addressed by him, Nala dwelt there, honored, in the city of Ṛtuparṇa, together with Vārṣṇeya and Jīvala.
t.3.64.9: Living there, the king kept thinking of the princess of Vidarbha, and every evening, without fail, he would recite this one verse.
t.3.64.11: As the king spoke thus in the night, Jīvala said to him: "Who is this woman for whom you constantly grieve? I wish to hear it, Bāhuka."
t.3.64.10: Where now does that poor woman lie, tormented by hunger and thirst and worn out, remembering that foolish man? Or whom does she wait upon today?
t.3.64.13: For some reason that foolish man was separated from her, and, parted from her, the dull-witted one wanders about, tormented by misery.
t.3.64.12: King Nala said to him: “A certain man of dull understanding had a woman whom he held in high esteem, and he was bound to her ever more firmly.”
t.3.64.15: Wandering over the whole earth, he, undeserving of such a fate, dwells wherever he happens to find some refuge, remembering that sorrow again and again.
t.3.64.14: Burning with grief day and night, he never rested; and at nightfall, remembering her, he would sing a single verse.
t.3.64.16: But that woman, who followed that man into the forest even in his hardship, was abandoned by him, a man of little merit; it would be a hard thing if she is still alive.
t.3.64.17: Alone, a young girl, ignorant of the paths, unaccustomed to such a plight, and overcome by hunger and thirst, it will be hard indeed if she survives.
t.3.64.18: In the great and dreadful forest, ever roamed by beasts of prey, I was abandoned by him, that man of little merit and dull understanding, O sir.
t.3.64.19: Thus the king of the Niṣadhas, ever remembering Damayantī, dwelt unrecognized in the palace of that king.
